question: Which of the following is considered an absolute contraindication for a planned home delivery?

options.A: Previous caesarean section delivery
options.B: Mild nausea during the first trimester
options.C: History of a normal vaginal delivery
options.D: Singleton pregnancy at 38 weeks gestation

explanation: A prior uterine scar carries the risk of uterine rupture during labor, necessitating immediate access to surgical facilities. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T8#GNS225_U3_T8_h4)

question: Why is a twin gestation classified as a high-risk condition unsuitable for home birth?

options.A: It prevents the mother from experiencing any uterine contractions
options.B: It always results in post-term pregnancy lasting beyond 43 weeks
options.C: It frequently leads to complications like malpresentation and postpartum hemorrhage
options.D: It automatically causes chronic renal failure in the pregnant woman

explanation: Multiple gestations require advanced neonatal resuscitation readiness and immediate surgical backup for the second twin if complications arise. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T8#GNS225_U3_T8_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing Leopold's maneuvers during an antenatal assessment?

options.A: To calculate the precise gestational age in weeks
options.B: To measure the exact volume of amniotic fluid
options.C: To detect chromosomal abnormalities in the fetus
options.D: To determine fetal lie, presentation, and position

explanation: Leopold's maneuvers involve systematic abdominal palpation to ascertain how the fetus is situated inside the uterus. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T8#GNS225_U3_T8_h5)

question: Why is checking the packed cell volume (PCV) especially critical during antenatal screening in Nigeria?

options.A: To confirm the exact date of conception and expected delivery
options.B: To screen for gestational diabetes mellitus and high blood sugar
options.C: To measure the clotting factor levels in the third trimester
options.D: To detect severe anemia that impairs tolerance to normal intrapartum blood loss

explanation: Anemic mothers have low reserves and can easily progress to cardiovascular collapse from standard postpartum blood loss. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T8#GNS225_U3_T8_h5)

question: Which factor represents a critical environmental requirement when assessing a home for potential childbirth?

options.A: Presence of an air-conditioned surgical suite
options.B: Access to a mechanical ventilator and oxygen tanks
options.C: Proximity to a private diagnostic laboratory
options.D: Availability of clean water and adequate lighting

explanation: Basic hygiene requires clean water, and safe delivery management requires adequate lighting, especially if labor occurs at night. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T8#GNS225_U3_T8_h6)

question: What is the main purpose of conducting a social assessment of the household before approving a home birth?

options.A: To evaluate the financial net worth and income of the extended family
options.B: To ensure family support and active cooperation with emergency plans
options.C: To verify that the pregnant woman is the head of the household
options.D: To determine the architectural layout and size of the family house

explanation: Family dynamics heavily influence decision-making during emergencies; supportive household members are essential for timely referral if complications arise. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T8#GNS225_U3_T8_h6)

question: What essential component must be included in every home birth plan to handle unexpected crises?

options.A: A written guarantee that no complications will occur during labor
options.B: A backup set of surgical instruments for emergency caesarean section
options.C: A clearly defined emergency referral pathway and transport plan
options.D: A signed agreement for an immediate blood transfusion at home

explanation: Because emergencies can arise without warning, pre-arranged transport and a designated receiving hospital save critical minutes. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T8#GNS225_U3_T8_h7)

question: Why is it important to contact the receiving health facility before transferring a patient experiencing an obstetric emergency?

options.A: To negotiate the exact hospital bill before the ambulance departs
options.B: To ensure the receiving team is prepared and waiting with necessary resources
options.C: To reserve a specific private recovery ward for the newborn baby
options.D: To check if the doctor is currently on a scheduled meal break

explanation: Advance communication prevents treatment delays upon arrival, ensuring blood products, operating theaters, or resuscitation gear are ready. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T8#GNS225_U3_T8_h7)

question: What must the nurse do if a low-risk patient insists on a home delivery after receiving thorough counseling on its risks?

options.A: Refuse to provide any further prenatal care or check-ups
options.B: Secure informed consent and finalize a detailed emergency transport plan
options.C: Ignore the patient's preference and force a hospital admission
options.D: Threaten the patient with immediate discharge from the antenatal clinic

explanation: Patients have the right to make informed choices about their care; the nurse's role is to ensure safety measures and consent are documented. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T8#GNS225_U3_T8_h8)

question: Which of the following best describes the legal and professional purpose of documentation during pregnancy screening?

options.A: To prove that the healthcare provider made all decisions for the patient
options.B: To provide insurance companies with reasons to deny maternal claims
options.C: To maintain an accurate record of clinical findings and ensure continuity of care
options.D: To fulfill a bureaucratic formality without any clinical relevance

explanation: Thorough documentation creates a legal and clinical timeline that guides future care providers and protects patient safety. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T8#GNS225_U3_T8_h8)

question: What is the primary objective of family planning programs?

options.A: Enabling individuals to decide the spacing and timing of births
options.B: Ensuring every family has at least four children
options.C: Eliminating the need for maternal and child health clinics
options.D: Controlling the exact gender distribution of offspring

explanation: Family planning centers on reproductive autonomy, allowing people to choose when and if they want children. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T1#GNS225_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why is universal access to family planning considered a public health priority?

options.A: It removes the need for antenatal care services
options.B: It guarantees economic equality for every household
options.C: It directly correlates with lower maternal mortality and improved child survival
options.D: It completely eradicates infectious diseases in developing nations

explanation: Controlling birth spacing prevents high-risk pregnancies, which drastically improves survival rates for both mothers and infants. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T1#GNS225_U3_T1_h1)

question: An interpregnancy interval of less than how many months is generally associated with increased health risks for the mother and child?

options.A: Forty-eight months
options.B: Thirty-six months
options.C: Sixteen months
options.D: Eighteen months

explanation: Evidence shows that spacing pregnancies less than eighteen apart fails to give the maternal body sufficient recovery time, raising complication rates. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T1#GNS225_U3_T1_h2)

question: How does closely spacing pregnancies directly impact maternal physiological status?

options.A: It depletes vital nutrient stores such as iron and folate
options.B: It builds permanent immunity against gestational diabetes
options.C: It accelerates the natural postpartum healing process
options.D: It permanently strengthens the muscular walls of the uterus

explanation: Carrying a pregnancy requires massive nutritional output, and rapid succession without replenishment leads to severe deficiencies. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T1#GNS225_U3_T1_h2)

question: What physical characteristic of cervical mucus indicates peak fertility during the menstrual cycle?

options.A: Brownish, foul-smelling, and viscous
options.B: Clear, stretchy, and resembling raw egg white
options.C: Thick, sticky, and opaque white
options.D: Dry, flaky, and sparse in volume

explanation: Fertile cervical mucus becomes watery, stretchy, and clear to help facilitate sperm transport into the upper reproductive tract. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T1#GNS225_U3_T1_h3)

question: Why does the basal body temperature rise slightly following ovulation?

options.A: Estrogen surges stimulate the hypothalamus to generate systemic heat
options.B: Progesterone released by the corpus luteum elevates resting body temperature
options.C: Increased physical activity during the luteal phase warms the core body
options.D: Implantation of the fertilized ovum triggers an inflammatory fever response

explanation: Progesterone is a thermogenic hormone, causing a measurable shift in basal body temperature right after an egg is released. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T1#GNS225_U3_T1_h3)

question: Which of the following is a unique clinical advantage of barrier contraceptive methods over hormonal alternatives?

options.A: They regulate erratic menstrual bleeding patterns effectively
options.B: They require no active participation during sexual intercourse
options.C: They completely eliminate the risk of primary dysmenorrhea
options.D: They offer significant protection against sexually transmitted infections

explanation: Physical barriers like condoms create a block that stops pathogens from transmitting between partners, which hormonal methods cannot do. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T1#GNS225_U3_T1_h4)

question: What is a primary clinical limitation associated with using chemical spermicides alone for birth control?

options.A: They induce severe systemic hypertension in hypertensive clients
options.B: They have lower contraceptive efficacy and can irritate mucosal tissue
options.C: They cause permanent blockage of the fallopian tubes
options.D: They require minor surgical incision for proper insertion

explanation: Spermicides have high failure rates when used independently and frequent application can cause local irritation, increasing infection risks. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T1#GNS225_U3_T1_h4)

question: How frequently must an injectable progestin contraceptive like depot medroxyprogesterone acetate typically be administered?

options.A: Every three months
options.B: Every single week
options.C: Every six months
options.D: Every five years

explanation: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate injections provide effective contraceptive coverage when administered intramuscularly or subcutaneously every twelve weeks. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T1#GNS225_U3_T1_h5)

question: Which primary mechanism do combined oral contraceptive pills use to prevent pregnancy?

options.A: Destruction of existing ova within the ovarian cortex
options.B: Permanent ablation of the functional endometrial layer
options.C: Immediate physical neutralization of deposited spermatozoa
options.D: Suppression of ovulation by inhibiting gonadotropin release

explanation: The synthetic hormones in combined pills stop the pituitary gland from releasing the surge of hormones needed to trigger ovulation. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T1#GNS225_U3_T1_h5)

question: What is the mechanism by which a copper intrauterine device primarily exerts its contraceptive effect?

options.A: Releasing high systemic doses of estrogen to block ovulation
options.B: Completely dissolving the myometrium over time
options.C: Triggering a local inflammatory response that is toxic to sperm
options.D: Absorbing all menstrual blood to prevent passage

explanation: Copper ions create an environment inside the uterus that impairs sperm motility and viability, preventing fertilization. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T1#GNS225_U3_T1_h6)

question: A male client who recently underwent a vasectomy asks if he can immediately stop using backup contraception. What is the correct nursing response?

options.A: No, vasectomies have a high spontaneous reversal rate within the first month
options.B: Yes, sterility is achieved immediately once the surgical sutures dissolve
options.C: Yes, as long as he takes oral antibiotics for the first week post-surgery
options.D: No, remaining sperm stored above the surgical site must clear through multiple ejaculations

explanation: It takes several weeks and multiple ejaculations to clear residual sperm remaining in the vas deferens past the surgical ligation point. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T1#GNS225_U3_T1_h6)

question: Which standardized clinical tool is primarily utilized by healthcare providers to assess the safety of specific contraceptive methods for clients with underlying medical conditions?

options.A: Glasgow Coma Scale
options.B: Apgar scoring scale
options.C: Partograph monitoring sheet
options.D: Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use

explanation: The Medical Eligibility Criteria guide provides evidence-based recommendations on whether clients with various health conditions can use specific methods safely. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T1#GNS225_U3_T1_h7)

question: Why is proactive counseling regarding potential side effects essential during the initial family planning visit?

options.A: It guarantees that the client will never experience irregular bleeding
options.B: It eliminates the need for any follow-up clinical appointments
options.C: It prevents clients from abandoning their chosen method due to unexpected changes
options.D: It legally transfers all liability for adverse drug reactions to the patient

explanation: Clients who know what side effects to expect are far less likely to panic and discontinue their contraceptive method prematurely. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T1#GNS225_U3_T1_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common misconception regarding modern contraceptives in many Nigerian communities?

options.A: They cause babies to be born with physical abnormalities
options.B: They promote illicit sexual behavior among adolescents
options.C: They lead to permanent infertility after discontinuation
options.D: They help reduce maternal mortality and space births safely

explanation: Reducing maternal mortality is a scientifically proven benefit of family planning, not a myth or misconception. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T1#GNS225_U3_T1_h8)

question: What is the most effective strategy for a nurse to address patriarchal and cultural resistance to family planning in a rural community?

options.A: Discontinuing community outreach until cultural norms shift naturally
options.B: Distributing contraceptives secretly without telling the partners or family
options.C: Filing formal complaints against community elders who oppose clinics
options.D: Engaging male partners and community leaders through respectful educational dialogue

explanation: Involving key decision-makers helps build local trust, correct misunderstandings, and foster supportive environments for reproductive health. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T1#GNS225_U3_T1_h8)

question: What is the primary objective of managing an obstetric emergency in a community setting?

options.A: Surgical correction of anatomical defects
options.B: Routine monitoring of labor progression
options.C: Complete recovery at the primary health center
options.D: Immediate stabilization and urgent referral

explanation: Because advanced surgical facilities are absent in community settings, the main priority is keeping the mother and baby stable while arranging rapid transfer to a higher-level facility. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T12#GNS225_U3_T12_h1)

question: Why do obstetric emergencies present an exceptionally high risk during rural community births?

options.A: Overuse of electronic fetal monitoring devices in homes
options.B: Strict adherence to hospital protocols by family members
options.C: Delayed access to advanced surgical and blood transfusion services
options.D: Routine availability of potent oxytocic drugs without supervision

explanation: Geographical isolation and transport barriers mean that life-threatening conditions like severe hemorrhage or uterine rupture cannot be surgically managed on-site, heightening mortality risks. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T12#GNS225_U3_T12_h1)

question: Which vital sign measurement serves as a critical red flag for potential maternal shock in a community setting?

options.A: Systolic blood pressure of 110 mmHg
options.B: Pulse rate exceeding 100 beats per minute
options.C: Body temperature of 36.5 degrees Celsius
options.D: Respiratory rate of 14 breaths per minute

explanation: Tachycardia is often the earliest physiological sign of compensatory mechanisms responding to acute blood loss or systemic infection. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T12#GNS225_U3_T12_h2)

question: A postpartum woman in a community clinic appears extremely lethargic and confused two hours after delivery. What does this behavioral change most likely suggest?

options.A: Normal physiological exhaustion following labor
options.B: Standard psychological adaptation to motherhood
options.C: Transient side effects of prophylactic oxytocin
options.D: Cerebral hypoxia or severe hemorrhagic shock

explanation: Altered mental status in a postpartum setting indicates inadequate brain perfusion due to blood loss or oxygen deprivation, requiring urgent intervention. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T12#GNS225_U3_T12_h2)

question: What is the immediate first-line physical maneuver for managing primary postpartum hemorrhage?

options.A: Application of a lower abdominal binder
options.B: Firm external or bimanual uterine massage
options.C: Immediate digital exploration of the cervix
options.D: Gentle traction on the umbilical cord

explanation: Uterine massage stimulates the myometrium to contract, compressing open blood vessels at the placental site to control bleeding. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T12#GNS225_U3_T12_h3)

question: Why are digital vaginal examinations strictly contraindicated when managing a patient with suspected placenta previa in the community?

options.A: It stimulates premature uterine contractions that accelerate active labor
options.B: It can disrupt placental attachment and provoke massive, life-threatening hemorrhage
options.C: It introduces bacterial pathogens that cause rapid postpartum endometritis
options.D: It causes severe pain that worsens maternal hypertensive spikes

explanation: Palpating through the cervix when the placenta is low-lying can directly tear placental blood vessels, worsening the hemorrhage. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T12#GNS225_U3_T12_h3)

question: What is the drug of choice for managing and preventing recurrent eclamptic seizures?

options.A: Magnesium sulfate
options.B: Hydralazine
options.C: Nifedipine
options.D: Diazepam

explanation: Magnesium sulfate is proven superior to other anticonvulsants for controlling eclamptic fits without causing profound maternal or fetal central nervous system depression. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T12#GNS225_U3_T12_h4)

question: A patient receiving magnesium sulfate therapy for severe pre-eclampsia develops a respiratory rate of 10 breaths per minute and absent knee-jerk reflexes. What is the most appropriate immediate nursing action?

options.A: Withhold further magnesium sulfate and prepare calcium gluconate
options.B: Encourage the patient to perform deep breathing exercises
options.C: Administer an immediate extra dose of magnesium sulfate intravenously
options.D: Increase the rate of the intravenous maintenance fluid infusion

explanation: Absent reflexes and respiratory depression are classic signs of magnesium toxicity; the drug must be stopped immediately and the antidote administered. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T12#GNS225_U3_T12_h4)

question: Which physical maneuver involves hyperflexing the mother's legs against her abdomen to relieve shoulder dystocia?

options.A: Kristeller maneuver
options.B: McRoberts maneuver
options.C: Zavanelli maneuver
options.D: Ritgen maneuver

explanation: The McRoberts maneuver flattens the sacrum and rotates the symphysis pubis cephalad, freeing the impacted anterior shoulder. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T12#GNS225_U3_T12_h5)

question: Why is forceful downward traction on the fetal head strictly avoided when managing shoulder dystocia?

options.A: It induces severe postpartum uterine atony in the mother
options.B: It prematurely detaches the placenta from the uterine wall
options.C: It exacerbates shoulder impaction and causes permanent brachial plexus injury
options.D: It increases the risk of maternal perineal lacerations to the fourth degree

explanation: Pulling downward stretches the nerves of the brachial plexus and jams the shoulder more tightly behind the pubic bone. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T12#GNS225_U3_T12_h5)

question: What is the immediate life-saving physical action required when an umbilical cord prolapse is diagnosed?

options.A: Gentle reinsertion of the protruding cord back into the uterus
options.B: Application of warm compresses over the maternal perineum
options.C: Manual elevation of the presenting fetal part off the cord
options.D: Immediate administration of high-dose intravenous oxytocin

explanation: Lifting the baby's head or body off the cord relieves compression and restores blood and oxygen flow to the fetus until delivery. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T12#GNS225_U3_T12_h6)

question: Which clinical presentation is most characteristic of a complete uterine rupture during labor?

options.A: Hyperactive uterine contractions accompanied by early fetal heart decelerations
options.B: Gradual onset of mild cramping accompanied by a low-grade maternal fever
options.C: Sudden severe tearing pain, cessation of contractions, and maternal shock
options.D: Pain-free vaginal spotting with a soft, non-tender uterine fundus

explanation: When the uterus ruptures, the muscle tears open, causing sharp tearing pain, loss of tone and contractions, and rapid bleeding into the abdomen. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T12#GNS225_U3_T12_h6)

question: Within what timeframe should newborn resuscitation ideally be initiated if the infant fails to breathe spontaneously?

options.A: Within half an hour
options.B: The golden minute
options.C: Within ten minutes
options.D: After five minutes

explanation: The first 60 seconds of life are crucial for initiating ventilation to prevent permanent hypoxic-ischemic organ damage in a compromised newborn. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T12#GNS225_U3_T12_h7)

question: What is the recommended ventilation rate when performing bag-mask ventilation on a distressed newborn?

options.A: 120 to 140 breaths per minute
options.B: 40 to 60 breaths per minute
options.C: 80 to 100 breaths per minute
options.D: 10 to 20 breaths per minute

explanation: Newborn physiology requires a rapid respiratory rate during resuscitation to match normal neonatal metabolic demands and clear lung fluid. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T12#GNS225_U3_T12_h7)

question: What critical component must accompany an obstetric referral from a community clinic to a hospital?

options.A: The family consent form signed by village elders
options.B: A written referral note detailing clinical findings and treatments given
options.C: Routine laboratory specimens collected prior to departure
options.D: Cash payment to cover emergency surgical fees at the destination

explanation: A clear referral note prevents duplication of tests, informs receiving clinicians of interventions already performed, and ensures continuity of care. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T12#GNS225_U3_T12_h8)

question: In the context of the three-delays model of maternal mortality, what does the second delay refer to?

options.A: Delays by the pregnant woman in deciding to seek professional healthcare
options.B: Delays in reaching a medical facility due to transport and geographical barriers
options.C: Delays in diagnosing hypertensive disorders during antenatal visits
options.D: Delays in receiving appropriate medical treatment once inside the hospital

explanation: The second delay involves transport logistics, road networks, and geographical distance separating the community from a functional health facility. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T12#GNS225_U3_T12_h8)

question: Why is post-crisis documentation emphasized following a community obstetric emergency?

options.A: It ensures legal protection and continuity of clinical handover
options.B: It serves as a replacement for verbal communication with doctors
options.C: It guarantees financial compensation from government agencies
options.D: It eliminates the need for future antenatal appointments

explanation: Precise records document the timing of interventions, medications administered, and patient responses, protecting staff and guiding ongoing hospital management. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T12#GNS225_U3_T12_h9)

question: What is the primary purpose of conducting community-level near-miss audits after managing a severe obstetric emergency?

options.A: To analyze system bottlenecks and improve future emergency response protocols
options.B: To calculate exact insurance payouts for families affected by complications
options.C: To assign personal blame to staff members who committed clinical errors
options.D: To reduce the frequency of routine antenatal clinic attendance

explanation: Near-miss audits provide valuable data on system strengths and weaknesses without the tragedy of a maternal death, guiding quality improvement. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T12#GNS225_U3_T12_h9)

question: What is the primary focus of Infant Welfare Services in primary healthcare settings?

options.A: Long-term inpatient rehabilitation
options.B: Disease prevention and health promotion
options.C: Surgical interventions for congenital anomalies
options.D: Emergency trauma care for children

explanation: Infant welfare clinics prioritize keeping well babies well through preventive measures, routine monitoring, and health education rather than acute or surgical hospital care. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T2#GNS225_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why is growth surveillance considered a core pillar of infant welfare clinics?

options.A: It replaces the need for routine childhood immunizations
options.B: It is required primarily for hospital administrative records
options.C: It allows early detection of developmental delays and malnutrition
options.D: It determines the exact adult height of the child

explanation: Regular tracking of physical growth helps healthcare providers spot faltering growth or developmental issues long before severe clinical manifestations appear. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T2#GNS225_U3_T2_h1)

question: At approximately what age should a normal infant be able to sit unsupported?

options.A: 6 months
options.B: 12 months
options.C: 10 months
options.D: 2 months

explanation: Trunk control typically strengthens enough by six months of age for an infant to maintain a sitting position without external support. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T2#GNS225_U3_T2_h2)

question: A 10-month-old infant seen at the clinic cannot yet bear weight on the legs or sit without support. What does this observation suggest?

options.A: A temporary phase related to teething discomfort
options.B: A potential developmental delay requiring further evaluation
options.C: An expected finding for an infant of this specific age group
options.D: A normal variation that requires no clinical follow-up

explanation: Failing to sit unsupported or bear weight by 10 months falls well outside normal developmental windows and warrants a thorough clinical assessment. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T2#GNS225_U3_T2_h2)

question: What is the recommended duration for exclusive breastfeeding according to global health guidelines?

options.A: The first six months of life
options.B: The first three months of life
options.C: Until the first tooth erupts
options.D: The entire first year of life

explanation: Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months provides optimal nutrition and protection against common infections without needing water or other foods. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T2#GNS225_U3_T2_h3)

question: Why must complementary foods be introduced around the age of six months?

options.A: Infants completely lose their sucking reflex at this exact age
options.B: Renal maturity prevents the digestion of breast milk proteins after six months
options.C: Mothers typically return to work and stop producing milk entirely
options.D: Breast milk alone is no longer sufficient to meet growing iron and energy needs

explanation: As the infant grows rapidly, nutritional demands—particularly for iron and total calories—outpace what breast milk alone can supply. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T2#GNS225_U3_T2_h3)

question: Which vaccines are typically administered at birth in the standard immunization schedule?

options.A: Measles and Yellow Fever
options.B: Pentavalent and Rotavirus
options.C: Inactivated Polio Vaccine and PCV
options.D: BCG, OPV 0, and Hepatitis B

explanation: At birth, infants receive BCG against tuberculosis, OPV zero for polio, and a birth dose of Hepatitis B before leaving the health facility. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T2#GNS225_U3_T2_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of maintaining a strict cold chain for vaccines?

options.A: To accelerate the absorption rate of the antigen into the muscle
options.B: To preserve the potency and effectiveness of the biological product
options.C: To make the injection less painful when administered to the infant
options.D: To prevent the physical vials from melting in tropical climates

explanation: Vaccines are sensitive biological substances that degrade and lose efficacy if exposed to improper temperatures outside the cold chain range. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T2#GNS225_U3_T2_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of plotting anthropometric measurements on a growth chart during clinic visits?

options.A: To monitor longitudinal health trends and detect faltering growth early
options.B: To determine the precise chronological age of teething
options.C: To diagnose specific genetic disorders without laboratory testing
options.D: To calculate the exact caloric intake required for the next month

explanation: Serial plotting of weight and length exposes trajectory changes, highlighting early malnutrition or chronic illness before acute symptoms present. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T2#GNS225_U3_T2_h5)

question: Which physical finding during a routine infant assessment warrants immediate clinical concern?

options.A: Eruption of the first lower central incisor
options.B: A sunken or abnormally bulging fontanelle
options.C: Desquamation of newborn skin in the first week
options.D: Mild physiological jaundice fading by day seven

explanation: A sunken fontanelle often points to dehydration, while a bulging one can indicate increased intracranial pressure, both requiring urgent evaluation. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T2#GNS225_U3_T2_h5)

question: What is the immediate priority in managing an infant with acute watery diarrhoea?

options.A: Administering strong broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.B: Stopping all forms of breastfeeding immediately
options.C: Preventing dehydration with oral rehydration salts
options.D: Providing high-dose intravenous iron therapy

explanation: Fluid and electrolyte loss from diarrhoea is the most dangerous aspect, making prompt oral rehydration the primary lifesaving intervention. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T2#GNS225_U3_T2_h6)

question: Which sign represents a general danger sign requiring emergency triage in an infant?

options.A: Spitting up small amounts of milk after a feed
options.B: Inability to breastfeed or drink fluids
options.C: Mild low-grade fever after a routine immunization
options.D: Slight nasal congestion without respiratory distress

explanation: An infant who cannot feed or drink is severely compromised and requires urgent hospital-level assessment and stabilization. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T2#GNS225_U3_T2_h6)

question: What is a primary objective of maternal health education during infant welfare visits?

options.A: Enabling mothers to diagnose complex surgical conditions independently
options.B: Empowering caregivers to recognize early illness signs and practice hygiene
options.C: Replacing the need for scheduled professional immunization visits
options.D: Training mothers to perform routine laboratory blood tests at home

explanation: Educating mothers equips them with practical skills to maintain safe home environments and seek timely help when health changes occur. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T2#GNS225_U3_T2_h7)

question: Why is teaching home-based preventative strategies like using insecticide-treated nets so crucial in infant care?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for clinic-based immunization
options.B: It prevents all forms of acute gastrointestinal infections
options.C: Mosquito nets also function as thermal regulators for neonates
options.D: Infants are highly vulnerable to vector-borne diseases like malaria

explanation: Malaria carries severe risks in infancy, making physical barrier protection through treated nets a vital component of home-based prevention. [learn more](GNS225_U3_T2#GNS225_U3_T2_h7)

question: What is the primary focus of domiciliary midwifery practice?

options.A: Conducting research on herbal remedies during pregnancy
options.B: Operating primary health care clinics in rural settlements
options.C: Providing maternity care within the client's private home
options.D: Managing complex surgical obstetric emergencies exclusively

question: Why do many pregnant women in Nigeria continue to utilize domiciliary midwifery services?

question: Which regulatory body governs the professional practice of midwives in Nigeria?

question: How did maternal care at home evolve historically in Nigeria before orthodox midwifery?

question: Which of the following conditions is an absolute contraindication for a planned home delivery?

question: Which drug is essential to include in a domiciliary midwifery emergency kit for the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage?

question: Why is pre-inspection of the home environment essential before scheduling a domiciliary confinement?

question: What is the primary tool used by midwives to monitor the active progress of labor and maternal-fetal well-being?

question: Why should vaginal examinations be performed sparingly during home labor management?

question: At what specific time intervals is the Apgar score routinely assessed for a newborn?

question: A newborn delivered at home is limp, cyanotic, and makes no respiratory effort after thorough drying and gentle stimulation. What is the immediate priority intervention?

question: What is the primary purpose of early postnatal home visits by the midwife?

question: Who bears legal and professional liability for midwifery care provided during a planned home delivery?

question: What is the primary purpose of home-based antenatal care?

question: A nurse is preparing to assist a client with lower limb weakness from a wheelchair to a nearby armchair. What is the most critical safety action to take first?

question: How can participation in peer support groups benefit an individual coping with a newly diagnosed physical disability?

question: A widow presents to the clinic with severe scalp infections and abrasions after completing traditional mourning rites. Which specific practice is most likely responsible?

question: What is a frequent psychological consequence experienced by widows subjected to severe public scrutiny and physical deprivation during mourning?

question: A newly bereaved widow arrives at the community health center exhibiting signs of malnutrition, severe joint pain from sleeping on bare floors, and depressive withdrawal. What primary clinical understanding should guide the nurse's initial assessment?

question: What is the primary approach community health nurses should use when caring for a survivor of FGM?

question: A community health nurse is designing an outreach program in a rural Nigerian community to address FGM. Which strategy represents the most effective preventive approach?

question: What is a primary financial motivation for some healthcare workers to perform medicalised FGM?

question: A nurse agrees to perform a ritual nick on a newborn to prevent the family from seeking a traditional circumciser. What underlying rationale influences this decision?

question: Which classification of FGM involves the narrowing of the vaginal orifice through the creation of a covering seal?

question: What is a common misconception held by clinicians who perform symbolic or minimal cuts during FGM?

question: Which intervention strategy is considered the most effective in the hierarchy of controls?

question: In the Epidemiological Triad, what does the 'host' refer to?

options.A: The physical climate and weather conditions of a region
options.B: The microbial pathogen causing the infection
options.C: The human or animal that harbors the causal agent and has variable susceptibility
options.D: The hospital facility providing treatment

explanation: The host is the human or animal harboring the agent, whose susceptibility is influenced by factors like age, immunity, and health status. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T1#GNS313_U1_T1_h5)

question: How does an environmental factor contribute to disease within the Epidemiological Triad framework?

options.A: It acts as the biological organism that directly causes genetic mutations.
options.B: It encompasses external physical, biological, and socioeconomic conditions that affect transmission and host vulnerability.
options.C: It determines the exact blood type of every individual in the population.
options.D: It serves as the pharmaceutical treatment administered by nurses.

explanation: The environment includes all external factors surrounding the host and agent that influence disease transmission and host susceptibility. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T1#GNS313_U1_T1_h5)

question: What key action did John Snow take during the 1854 cholera outbreak in London that established him as a pioneer of epidemiology?

options.A: He administered broad-spectrum antibiotics to all infected patients.
options.B: He mapped the cholera cases and removed the handle from the contaminated Broad Street water pump.
options.C: He quarantined the entire city of London for forty days.
options.D: He proved that miasma in the air was the sole cause of cholera transmission.

explanation: John Snow mapped disease locations, identified the water pump as the source, and removed its handle to stop the cholera outbreak. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T1#GNS313_U1_T1_h6)

question: How did Florence Nightingale contribute to the historical development of epidemiological and health statistics?

options.A: By using statistics during the Crimean War to prove that poor hospital sanitation caused excess soldier mortality
options.B: By inventing the first microscope to discover bacterial agents
options.C: By discovering the viral etiology of smallpox in military camps
options.D: By establishing the first pharmaceutical manufacturing plant in Europe

explanation: Nightingale used statistical records during the Crimean War to demonstrate that sanitation and ventilation were critical to reducing mortality. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T1#GNS313_U1_T1_h6)

question: How do community health nurses use epidemiological data during a community health assessment?

options.A: To diagnose individual psychiatric disorders in an inpatient ward
options.B: To identify which health issues and threats pose the greatest risk to the local population
options.C: To calculate the daily financial budget of a tertiary hospital
options.D: To prescribe surgical treatments for chronic diseases

explanation: Nurses use epidemiological data in assessments to identify major health threats and prioritize interventions for the community. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T1#GNS313_U1_T1_h7)

question: During a disease outbreak, such as Lassa fever, which specific epidemiological tasks might a nurse be involved in?

options.A: Contact tracing, isolation protocols, and surveillance reporting
options.B: Conducting major orthopedic surgeries in primary health clinics
options.C: Designing new architectural blueprints for regional hospitals
options.D: Performing routine dental extractions for school children

explanation: Nurses apply epidemiological principles during outbreaks by conducting contact tracing, enforcing isolation, and reporting surveillance data. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T1#GNS313_U1_T1_h7)

question: What term best describes an unexpected increase in disease cases within a specific, localized geographic area and time period?

options.A: Pandemic
options.B: Outbreak
options.C: Endemic
options.D: Syndrome

explanation: An outbreak specifically refers to a localized, unexpected surge of disease cases in a specific area and time frame. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T10#GNS313_U1_T10_h1)

question: Which of the following describes a disease that is constantly and predictably present at a baseline level in a specific region, such as malaria in West Africa?

options.A: Pandemic
options.B: Epidemic
options.C: Endemic
options.D: Outbreak

explanation: An endemic disease is one that remains constantly present at a baseline level within a specific geographic population. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T10#GNS313_U1_T10_h1)

question: In the epidemiological triangle, what does the 'agent' component represent?

options.A: The human or animal harboring the disease
options.B: The external sanitation and climate factors
options.C: The microorganism directly responsible for the disease
options.D: The vector carrying the pathogen across borders

explanation: The agent refers to the specific microorganism, such as a bacterium or virus, that directly causes the infectious disease. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T10#GNS313_U1_T10_h2)

question: Which of the following is an example of indirect disease transmission?

options.A: Direct skin-to-skin contact
options.B: Inhalation of large respiratory droplets during a face-to-face conversation
options.C: Drinking water contaminated with cholera bacteria
options.D: Kissing an infected individual

explanation: Waterborne transmission is a classic form of vehicle-mediated indirect transmission where an intermediary object or substance carries the pathogen. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T10#GNS313_U1_T10_h2)

question: What is the very first step typically taken when responding to a suspected disease outbreak?

options.A: Implementing quarantine measures for the entire state
options.B: Confirming the existence of an outbreak using baseline data
options.C: Publishing the final research report in a medical journal
options.D: Conducting a complex cohort study

explanation: The investigation begins by confirming that an actual outbreak exists by comparing current case numbers against expected baseline levels. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T10#GNS313_U1_T10_h3)

question: During an outbreak investigation, when should control and prevention measures ideally be implemented?

options.A: Only after the final investigation report is published
options.B: As soon as possible, without waiting for the investigation to conclude
options.C: Only after the definitive laboratory source is identified
options.D: After the epidemic curve has completely returned to zero

explanation: Control measures should be implemented immediately upon suspecting an outbreak to halt ongoing transmission and protect the public. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T10#GNS313_U1_T10_h3)

question: Why is a standardized case definition crucial during an outbreak investigation?

options.A: It ensures everyone counts the same phenomena consistently and accurately.
options.B: It replaces the need for laboratory testing entirely.
options.C: It guarantees that no new cases will ever occur.
options.D: It eliminates the need for environmental health inspections.

explanation: A standardized case definition ensures consistent classification of cases across all reporting sites, preventing data skewing. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T10#GNS313_U1_T10_h4)

question: How is a 'suspected' case typically characterized in an outbreak setting?

options.A: Verified exclusively through positive culture results
options.B: Meeting clinical signs and symptoms without definitive lab confirmation
options.C: Having no symptoms but living in the same country
options.D: Fully recovered and immune to the pathogen

explanation: A suspected case typically exhibits the clinical criteria of the illness but lacks definitive laboratory confirmation at that stage. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T10#GNS313_U1_T10_h4)

question: What does an epidemic curve (epi curve) visually represent?

options.A: The geographic distribution of hospitals across a country
options.B: The number of disease cases plotted over time by date of symptom onset
options.C: The financial cost of managing an outbreak per patient
options.D: The genetic mutation rate of a viral pathogen

explanation: An epi curve is a visual histogram showing the frequency of cases over time based on when symptoms began. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T10#GNS313_U1_T10_h5)

question: What type of outbreak pattern is typically indicated by a steep, single-peak epidemic curve followed by a downward slope?

options.A: A propagated outbreak spreading person-to-person
options.B: A continuous common-source outbreak
options.C: A point-source outbreak from a single exposure
options.D: An endemic baseline fluctuation

explanation: A point-source outbreak involves a single exposure event, resulting in a sharp, single peak on the histogram. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T10#GNS313_U1_T10_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of public health containment interventions during an outbreak?

options.A: To increase the mutation rate of the infectious agent
options.B: To break the chain of transmission and protect the public
options.C: To delay reporting data until the outbreak finishes naturally
options.D: To replace clinical nursing care with administrative tasks

explanation: Containment measures are specifically designed to interrupt transmission pathways and safeguard community health. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T10#GNS313_U1_T10_h6)

question: Which intervention is most appropriate for controlling a vector-borne disease like malaria?

options.A: Issuing boil-water advisories for municipal water supplies
options.B: Distributing insecticide-treated bed nets and vector control
options.C: Quarantining asymptomatic individuals in an isolated ward
options.D: Administering broad-spectrum antibiotics to the entire community

explanation: Vector-borne diseases are managed effectively by targeting the vectors directly, such as using insecticide-treated bed nets. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T10#GNS313_U1_T10_h6)

question: Why is community engagement essential during public health outbreak interventions?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any medical supplies or treatments.
options.B: It ensures interventions are culturally accepted and trusted by the local population.
options.C: It allows nurses to transfer all clinical responsibilities to community members.
options.D: It prevents the creation of epidemic curves.

explanation: Engaging communities builds trust, dispels myths, and ensures that public health measures are culturally respected and followed. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T10#GNS313_U1_T10_h7)

question: What is a major negative consequence of disease-related social stigma during an outbreak?

options.A: It causes patients to hide symptoms and delay seeking medical care.
options.B: It automatically improves community compliance with quarantine.
options.C: It enhances the accuracy of epidemic curve forecasting.
options.D: It accelerates the production of effective vaccines.

explanation: Stigma creates fear of isolation, causing individuals to conceal illness, which worsens community transmission. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T10#GNS313_U1_T10_h7)

question: When is an outbreak typically declared to be officially over?

options.A: Immediately after the first patient is discharged from the hospital
options.B: After a period equal to two incubation periods has passed without new cases
options.C: As soon as the media stops reporting on the event
options.D: When the initial case definition is revised for the first time

explanation: An outbreak is generally considered over when twice the incubation period of the pathogen passes with no new detected cases. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T10#GNS313_U1_T10_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of conducting an after-action review (AAR) following an outbreak?

options.A: To penalize healthcare workers who made clinical errors
options.B: To evaluate response performance and identify lessons for future preparedness
options.C: To re-open closed epidemiological triangles from past decades
options.D: To permanently close healthcare facilities in affected districts

explanation: An after-action review analyzes response strengths and weaknesses to improve preparedness for future health emergencies. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T10#GNS313_U1_T10_h8)

question: What is the primary focus of incidence in epidemiological studies?

options.A: Counting total existing cases of a chronic disease
options.B: Tracking the occurrence of new health events over a specified period
options.C: Measuring the total number of deaths in a hospital
options.D: Determining the total population size of a community

explanation: Incidence specifically measures the transition from a healthy state to a disease state by tracking newly diagnosed health events over a specified time frame. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h1)

question: Why is understanding incidence particularly important for community health nurses in Nigeria?

options.A: It helps them manage individual patient billing
options.B: It assists in tracking outbreaks like malaria and planning prevention strategies
options.C: It replaces the need for vital statistics collection
options.D: It dictates hospital bed architecture and design

explanation: By tracking incidence, nurses can identify active disease spread, such as malaria or Lassa fever outbreaks, and plan targeted interventions and resource allocation. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h1)

question: Which of the following correctly represents the numerator in the standard incidence formula?

options.A: Total existing cases in the population
options.B: Number of new cases of a disease during a specific period
options.C: Total population of the community
options.D: Number of recovered patients

explanation: The numerator for incidence calculations always consists strictly of the newly diagnosed cases occurring during the specified time frame. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h2)

question: When calculating the population at risk for a specific disease, who must be excluded from the denominator?

options.A: Individuals who are healthy and capable of contracting the disease
options.B: Individuals who already have the condition or lack the organ/system to contract it
options.C: Individuals who live in urban areas
options.D: Individuals who received a vaccine

explanation: The denominator must only include those at risk, meaning individuals who already have the condition or are anatomically immune must be excluded. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h2)

question: What is the primary difference between incidence and prevalence?

options.A: Incidence counts only new cases, while prevalence counts both old and new cases
options.B: Incidence measures mortality, while prevalence measures morbidity
options.C: Prevalence only applies to infectious diseases, while incidence applies to chronic conditions
options.D: There is no mathematical or conceptual difference between them

explanation: Incidence tracks the onset of new cases, whereas prevalence measures all existing cases (both old and new) in a population at a given time. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h3)

question: Why might a chronic disease like HIV have a high prevalence even if its incidence remains relatively stable?

options.A: Because patients recover completely within a few days
options.B: Because patients live with the condition for a long duration of time
options.C: Because no new cases are ever diagnosed
options.D: Because the disease has a 100% immediate mortality rate

explanation: Prevalence is influenced by disease duration; long-lasting chronic conditions accumulate over time, leading to high prevalence even with steady incidence rates. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h3)

question: Which of the following best describes cumulative incidence?

options.A: The speed of disease occurrence using person-years
options.B: The probability or risk of developing a disease over a specified time period in a closed population
options.C: The total number of existing chronic cases in a hospital
options.D: The mortality rate divided by the birth rate

explanation: Cumulative incidence represents the risk of disease development over time, requiring all individuals to be followed from the start to the finish of the observation period. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h4)

question: When is incidence density (incidence rate using person-time) particularly advantageous?

options.A: When studying a static, closed population with zero migration
options.B: When working with open or dynamic populations where individuals enter and leave the study at varying times
options.C: When calculating point prevalence during a one-day health survey
options.D: When counting total hospital admissions without regard to time

explanation: Incidence density utilizes person-time in the denominator, making it ideal for open populations where participants migrate, drop out, or enter at different times. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h4)

question: What is required in the denominator when calculating incidence density that is not required for cumulative incidence?

options.A: The total population at birth
options.B: The actual amount of person-time each individual contributes to the study
options.C: The total number of deaths recorded in the state
options.D: The financial cost of running the health facility

explanation: Incidence density uses person-time (such as person-years or months) in the denominator to account for the exact duration each person is observed at risk. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h5)

question: Which of the following factors can negatively skew incidence measurements in healthcare settings?

options.A: Consistent use of standardized diagnostic criteria
options.B: Rigorous record-keeping in primary healthcare clinics
options.C: Underreporting of new cases by rural health facilities
options.D: Accurate tracking of cohort entry criteria

explanation: Underreporting of new cases leads to inaccurate numerators, which can severely skew and underestimate the true incidence of a disease in a population. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h5)

question: How do environmental and socioeconomic factors influence disease incidence?

options.A: They have no impact on microbial transmission
options.B: Poor sanitation, overcrowding, and lack of clean water accelerate pathogen transmission and increase incidence
options.C: They solely decrease the incidence of chronic illnesses
options.D: They only affect hospital administrative costs

explanation: Inadequate sanitation, overcrowding, and contaminated water supplies facilitate the spread of pathogens, resulting in higher incidence rates. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h6)

question: What is an example of a seasonal factor that can influence incidence rates in regions like Nigeria?

options.A: The timing of national parliamentary elections
options.B: The onset of the rainy season increasing mosquito breeding and malaria incidence
options.C: Changes in international currency exchange rates
options.D: The implementation of hospital accreditation standards

explanation: Seasonal changes, such as the rainy season, promote vector breeding which directly correlates with a surge in malaria incidence. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of monitoring incidence rates within a disease surveillance system?

options.A: To calculate individual nurse salaries
options.B: To detect sudden spikes in new cases and signal potential disease outbreaks early
options.C: To determine hospital interior design layouts
options.D: To eliminate the need for patient medical records

explanation: Continuous monitoring of incidence helps public health professionals identify unusual increases in new cases, enabling early outbreak detection and rapid containment. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h7)

question: How do community health nurses in primary healthcare centers contribute to the Nigerian disease surveillance framework?

options.A: By logging and reporting new disease cases into the Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) system
options.B: By conducting international pharmaceutical research trials
options.C: By managing national healthcare financial budgets
options.D: By manufacturing vaccines locally

explanation: Nurses at PHC centers are frontline reporters who document and submit new case data to frameworks like the IDSR to support national surveillance. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T11#GNS313_U1_T11_h7)

question: What does prevalence measure in a population?

options.A: Only the development of new cases
options.B: All existing cases, both old and new
options.C: The rate of disease recovery
options.D: Only mortality rates

explanation: Prevalence measures all existing cases of a disease, including both old and new cases, within a specific population at a given time. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T12#GNS313_U1_T12_h1)

question: Why is prevalence data particularly useful for community health nurses?

options.A: It helps determine the total burden of disease to plan resource allocation and screening programs
options.B: It predicts exact individual lifespans
options.C: It tracks only newly infected patients in a hospital
options.D: It eliminates the need for public health policies

explanation: Understanding the total disease burden via prevalence helps nurses plan interventions, secure medications, and design targeted screening programs. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T12#GNS313_U1_T12_h1)

question: Which type of prevalence measures a condition at a single, specific point in time like a snapshot?

options.A: Period prevalence
options.B: Point prevalence
options.C: Cumulative incidence
options.D: Mortality prevalence

explanation: Point prevalence captures the exact disease status of a population at one specific point in time, acting like a snapshot. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T12#GNS313_U1_T12_h2)

question: When is period prevalence most useful to healthcare planners?

options.A: For diagnosing acute single-day trauma
options.B: For tracking chronic conditions with fluctuating symptoms over a time interval
options.C: For calculating exact birth weights
options.D: For measuring instant medication side effects

explanation: Period prevalence is ideal for chronic diseases with intermittent flare-ups because it counts cases present at any time during a specified interval. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T12#GNS313_U1_T12_h2)

question: In the standard prevalence formula, what does the numerator represent?

options.A: Only the newly diagnosed cases during a study
options.B: The total number of existing cases in a defined population at a specified time
options.C: The total population without the disease
options.D: The number of people who died from the disease

explanation: The numerator in a prevalence calculation is the total number of existing cases (both old and new) in the population at a specified time. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T12#GNS313_U1_T12_h3)

question: If a village of 2,000 people has 100 individuals suffering from a chronic ailment, what is the prevalence expressed per 1,000 population?
explanation: Dividing 100 by 2,000 gives 0.05. Multiplying 0.05 by a base of 1,000 yields a rate of 50 per 1,000 population. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T12#GNS313_U1_T12_h3)

question: Which of the following factors will cause an increase in the prevalence of a disease?

options.A: High cure rate and rapid recovery
options.B: High case-fatality rate
options.C: Longer duration of the disease and high incidence
options.D: Mass emigration of sick individuals

explanation: A high incidence of new cases combined with a long disease duration keeps patients ill longer, thereby increasing overall prevalence. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T12#GNS313_U1_T12_h4)

question: Why might a disease have a low prevalence despite having a high incidence?

options.A: If the disease has a very short duration or high mortality rate
options.B: If patients live with the condition for decades
options.C: If no one ever recovers from the illness
options.D: If the population size decreases to zero

explanation: If patients recover very quickly or die rapidly from the disease, they do not remain in the pool of existing cases, resulting in low prevalence. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T12#GNS313_U1_T12_h4)

question: How does incidence differ fundamentally from prevalence?

options.A: Incidence measures only old cases, while prevalence measures new cases.
options.B: Incidence measures the development of new cases, while prevalence measures all existing cases.
options.C: Incidence is expressed as a percentage, while prevalence is never calculated mathematically.
options.D: Incidence only applies to chronic diseases, while prevalence applies to acute illnesses.

explanation: Incidence tracks the onset of new cases representing risk, whereas prevalence captures the total burden of all existing cases at a given time. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T12#GNS313_U1_T12_h5)

question: Using the bathtub analogy, what does the water currently sitting in the tub represent?

options.A: Incidence
options.B: Mortality rate
options.C: Prevalence
options.D: Recovery rate

explanation: In the bathtub analogy, the total volume of water in the tub represents prevalence, while the water flowing from the tap represents incidence. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T12#GNS313_U1_T12_h5)

question: How do public health nurses primarily use prevalence data in community practice?

options.A: To identify high-risk groups, prioritize diagnoses, and allocate resources efficiently
options.B: To calculate individual patient medication dosages
options.C: To diagnose acute surgical emergencies in an operating room
options.D: To eliminate the need for community assessments

explanation: Prevalence data guides nurses in identifying vulnerable populations and directing public health resources to where the disease burden is highest. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T12#GNS313_U1_T12_h6)

question: What can tracking prevalence rates over multiple years help a community nurse determine?

options.A: The daily weather patterns affecting a hospital
options.B: The effectiveness and impact of long-term community health programs
options.C: The exact birth date of every community member
options.D: The personal financial income of patients

explanation: Sequential tracking of prevalence over time allows nurses to assess whether public health interventions are successfully lowering the disease burden. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T12#GNS313_U1_T12_h6)

question: Why is it difficult for prevalence studies to establish cause-and-effect relationships?

options.A: Because they measure existing cases, making it hard to determine if the risk factor preceded the disease
options.B: Because they only measure new cases over time
options.C: Because math formulas for prevalence are always inaccurate
options.D: Because they completely ignore population demographics

explanation: Prevalence captures existing cases at one time, creating temporality bias where it is unclear whether a risk factor came before or after the illness. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T12#GNS313_U1_T12_h7)

question: What type of bias occurs in prevalence studies when rapidly fatal conditions are underrepresented?

options.A: Recall bias
options.B: Survival bias
options.C: Selection bias
options.D: Interviewer bias

explanation: Survival bias happens because conditions with high mortality are missed in prevalence counts since patients die quickly before being surveyed. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T12#GNS313_U1_T12_h7)

question: Which population is noted as being particularly vulnerable to the high burden of communicable diseases in Nigeria?

options.A: Middle-aged corporate workers
options.B: Children under five and pregnant women
options.C: Retired military personnel
options.D: University undergraduate students

explanation: The text explicitly highlights children under five and pregnant women as vulnerable populations suffering substantially from communicable diseases in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T13#GNS313_U1_T13_h1)

question: What is identified as a major contributing factor to the persistence of communicable diseases in Nigeria?

options.A: Excessive access to clean water
options.B: Overcrowded housing and inadequate sanitation
options.C: Over-immunization of the population
options.D: Surplus funding in primary health care

explanation: Inadequate sanitation and overcrowded housing are highlighted as environmental and social factors that exacerbate disease transmission risks. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T13#GNS313_U1_T13_h1)

question: Which of the following describes the three components of the epidemiological triangle?

options.A: Agent, Host, Environment
options.B: Vector, Reservoir, Portal of Entry
options.C: Bacteria, Virus, Parasite
options.D: Source, Transmission, Susceptibility

explanation: The epidemiological triangle consists of three interactive components: the agent, the host, and the environment. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T13#GNS313_U1_T13_h2)

question: What is the primary significance of the chain of infection in healthcare practice?

options.A: It measures the exact incubation period of every known virus.
options.B: It details the financial cost of treating endemic infections.
options.C: Breaking any single link in the chain stops the spread of infection.
options.D: It identifies the exact geographic coordinates of a disease outbreak.

explanation: The text notes that breaking any single link in the chain stops the spread of infection, making it a crucial framework for interventions. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T13#GNS313_U1_T13_h2)

question: Which of the following is an example of indirect transmission via an inanimate object?

options.A: Sexual intercourse with an infected partner
options.B: Direct skin-to-skin touching during contact sports
options.C: Handling contaminated bed linens or surgical instruments
options.D: Coughing directly into someone's face at close range

explanation: Inanimate objects like bed linens and surgical instruments are known as fomites, which mediate indirect transmission. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T13#GNS313_U1_T13_h3)

question: Why is vector-borne transmission particularly important to study in the context of Nigeria?

options.A: Vectors are only found in cold, mountainous climates.
options.B: Vectors like mosquitoes transmit prevalent tropical diseases such as malaria.
options.C: Vectors rely solely on fomites to infect human hosts.
options.D: Vectors eliminate the need for an infectious agent.

explanation: The text states that vector-borne transmission is prominent in tropical regions like Nigeria, where vectors transmit pathogens like malaria and yellow fever. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T13#GNS313_U1_T13_h3)

question: During which phase of the natural history of disease do primary prevention measures operate?

options.A: Pathogenesis phase
options.B: Pre-pathogenesis phase
options.C: Clinical outcome phase
options.D: Rehabilitation phase

explanation: Primary prevention measures operate during the pre-pathogenesis phase, before the disease process has established in the host. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T13#GNS313_U1_T13_h4)

question: What defines the incubation period within the pathogenesis phase?

options.A: The time required for full recovery and rehabilitation
options.B: The period between exposure to an agent and the appearance of clinical signs and symptoms
options.C: The stage where chronic disability is permanently established
options.D: The interval during which primary prevention is administered

explanation: The text defines the incubation period as the time between exposure and the appearance of clinical signs and symptoms. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T13#GNS313_U1_T13_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of epidemiological surveillance in public health?

options.A: To punish healthcare workers who miss a diagnosis
options.B: The ongoing collection and analysis of health data to plan and evaluate public health practice
options.C: To replace standard clinical bedside nursing care
options.D: To manufacture pharmaceutical vaccines locally

explanation: Epidemiological surveillance is defined as the ongoing collection, analysis, interpretation, and dissemination of health data essential for public health practice. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T13#GNS313_U1_T13_h5)

question: How does an active surveillance system differ from a passive system?

options.A: Active surveillance relies on patients reporting their own symptoms online.
options.B: Active surveillance involves public health workers actively searching for cases in communities and facilities.
options.C: Active surveillance is only used for non-communicable chronic diseases.
options.D: Passive surveillance requires nurses to travel door-to-door daily.

explanation: In active surveillance, public health workers actively search out cases in communities or health facilities rather than waiting for routine reports. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T13#GNS313_U1_T13_h5)

question: Which of the following is a classic example of primary prevention for communicable diseases?

options.A: Administering routine childhood immunizations
options.B: Conducting malaria rapid diagnostic testing
options.C: Providing physical rehabilitation for polio survivors
options.D: Performing sputum smear microscopy for tuberculosis

explanation: Routine childhood immunization is a primary prevention strategy designed to prevent the occurrence of disease before it starts. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T13#GNS313_U1_T13_h6)

question: What is the primary objective of secondary prevention in communicable disease management?

options.A: To eliminate all vectors from the global environment
options.B: Early diagnosis and prompt treatment to halt disease progression
options.C: To provide long-term institutionalized rehabilitation exclusively
options.D: To manufacture new pharmacological antibiotics

explanation: Secondary prevention focuses on early diagnosis and prompt treatment to stop the disease from progressing and to prevent transmission. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T13#GNS313_U1_T13_h6)

question: Which role does a community health nurse fulfill when translating complex health information into culturally sensitive messages for local communities?

options.A: Epidemiologist
options.B: Educator
options.C: Laboratory scientist
options.D: Pharmacologist

explanation: As an educator, the nurse explains health concepts clearly and culturally sensitively to individuals and communities to promote healthy behaviors. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T13#GNS313_U1_T13_h7)

question: Why is collaboration with multidisciplinary teams important for community health nurses managing communicable diseases?

options.A: It removes all responsibilities of care from the nursing profession.
options.B: It ensures that preventive and treatment measures effectively bridge gaps in the healthcare system.
options.C: It is exclusively required for administrative paperwork.
options.D: It replaces the need for community engagement.

explanation: Collaborating with multidisciplinary teams helps bridge gaps in healthcare delivery, ensuring comprehensive and effective public health interventions. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T13#GNS313_U1_T13_h7)

question: What best describes an endemic disease within a population?

options.A: A sudden, unexpected spike in disease cases worldwide
options.B: A constant, predictable baseline presence of a disease in a specific area
options.C: A completely eradicated infection that occasionally returns
options.D: An infection that affects only travelers from other countries

explanation: An endemic disease is characterized by a constant and predictable baseline presence within a specific geographic area or population group over time. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T14#GNS313_U1_T14_h1)

question: Why is managing an endemic disease different from managing an epidemic?

options.A: Endemic diseases require long-term, sustained public health strategies rather than short emergency responses.
options.B: Endemic diseases never cause any mortality or morbidity.
options.C: Endemics only affect elderly populations.
options.D: Epidemics have a lower infection rate than endemics.

explanation: Because endemic diseases remain consistently present at a baseline level, they require long-term, sustained health planning rather than short-term emergency outbreak interventions. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T14#GNS313_U1_T14_h1)

question: What signals that a disease has transitioned from an endemic state to an epidemic?

options.A: A decrease in total cases below the historical average
options.B: A sudden, significant rise in cases above what is normally expected
options.C: The complete eradication of the infectious agent
options.D: The spread of the disease to every continent simultaneously

explanation: An epidemic is defined by a sudden and significant increase in disease frequency well above the normal baseline expected for that specific population. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T14#GNS313_U1_T14_h2)

question: What is the primary characteristic that separates a pandemic from an epidemic?

options.A: A pandemic involves higher mortality rates only.
options.B: A pandemic spreads across multiple countries or continents, affecting a large population.
options.C: A pandemic only occurs in rural farming communities.
options.D: A pandemic has a predictable and constant baseline.

explanation: While an epidemic can be localized or regional, a pandemic is characterized by its wide geographical spread across multiple countries or continents. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T14#GNS313_U1_T14_h2)

question: Which term describes a disease with a high infection rate beginning early in life, where nearly all children are infected and adults develop some immunity?

options.A: Pandemic
options.B: Hyperendemic
options.C: Holoendemic
options.D: Sporadic

explanation: Holoendemic diseases affect nearly all individuals starting early in life, resulting in adults having acquired immunity while children bear the brunt of severe illness. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T14#GNS313_U1_T14_h3)

question: How does a hyperendemic disease differ fundamentally from a holoendemic disease regarding affected populations?

options.A: Hyperendemic diseases affect all age groups equally without the specific acquired immunity profile seen in holoendemic conditions.
options.B: Hyperendemic diseases only affect the elderly.
options.C: Hyperendemic diseases disappear during the rainy season.
options.D: Hyperendemic diseases have zero mortality among children.

explanation: Hyperendemic diseases maintain a high incidence across all age groups equally, lacking the strong age-specific immunity gradient characteristic of holoendemic diseases. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T14#GNS313_U1_T14_h3)

question: Which rodent reservoir is primarily responsible for the transmission of Lassa fever, an endemic viral hemorrhagic fever in West Africa?

options.A: Anopheles mosquito
options.B: Mastomys natalensis rat
options.C: Black-legged tick
options.D: Tsetse fly

explanation: Lassa fever is endemic to parts of West Africa and is primarily transmitted to humans through contact with the excreta of the Mastomys natalensis rodent. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T14#GNS313_U1_T14_h4)

question: Which population group is particularly vulnerable to malaria in holoendemic regions of sub-Saharan Africa?

options.A: Adolescent males
options.B: Pregnant women and children under five
options.C: Elderly individuals living in urban centers
options.D: Infants over one year with full acquired immunity

explanation: Pregnant women and children under five suffer the heaviest clinical burden and highest morbidity from malaria in holoendemic sub-Saharan regions due to immature or compromised immunity. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T14#GNS313_U1_T14_h4)

question: Which of the following represents an environmental determinant that promotes the persistence of vector-borne endemic diseases?

options.A: High availability of modern hospitals
options.B: Stagnant water bodies and tropical rainfall patterns
options.C: Strict enforcement of building codes
options.D: Widespread access to potable piped water

explanation: Stagnant water and tropical rains provide ideal breeding sites for disease vectors such as mosquitoes, promoting the ongoing transmission of endemic infections. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T14#GNS313_U1_T14_h5)

question: How do cultural practices and health-seeking behaviors impact the transmission dynamics of endemic diseases?

options.A: They completely eliminate all forms of vector reproduction.
options.B: They can delay prompt medical diagnosis and treatment, allowing continuous pathogen circulation.
options.C: They guarantee 100% adherence to institutional immunization schedules.
options.D: They eliminate socioeconomic disparities.

explanation: Delayed diagnosis and reliance on traditional remedies due to cultural beliefs can keep infected individuals in the community longer, sustaining pathogen transmission. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T14#GNS313_U1_T14_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of integrated disease surveillance and response (IDSR) frameworks in nursing practice?

options.A: To punish healthcare workers who fail to treat patients quickly
options.B: To provide ongoing collection, analysis, and timely reporting of health data to guide control efforts
options.C: To restrict patient movement across international borders
options.D: To replace the need for clinical physical examinations

explanation: Surveillance frameworks ensure systematic data collection and timely reporting, enabling public health teams to monitor trends and respond effectively to endemic threats. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T14#GNS313_U1_T14_h6)

question: Which epidemiological metric measures the total number of existing cases of an endemic disease at a specific point in time?

options.A: Incidence rate
options.B: Prevalence rate
options.C: Mortality rate
options.D: Case fatality ratio

explanation: Prevalence rate refers to the total number of existing disease cases in a population at a given point in time, unlike incidence which measures only new cases. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T14#GNS313_U1_T14_h6)

question: Which nursing activity is classified as primary prevention for an endemic vector-borne disease?

options.A: Screening patients for active tuberculosis via sputum microscopy
options.B: Distributing insecticide-treated bed nets and educating on vector control
options.C: Administering antibiotics to cure advanced typhoid fever
options.D: Providing physical therapy for chronic lymphatic filariasis complications

explanation: Primary prevention involves measures implemented before disease occurs, such as using bed nets and vector control to stop transmission before infection happens. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T14#GNS313_U1_T14_h7)

question: What is the primary focus of secondary prevention in the management of endemic diseases?
